sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: Explains that untreated CIN2 or CIN3 lesions can progress to cervical cancer and describes the screen-and-treat approach, in which treatment follows soon after a positive screening test. It names the available screening tests (HPV test, VIA, cytology) and treatments (cryotherapy, LEEP, cold knife conization), and notes the guideline builds on earlier WHO guidance. It ends with research priorities and states that the recommendations apply to all women, with specific ones for women living with HIV.

sections.extract: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a premalignant lesion that may exist at any one of three stages: CIN1, CIN2, or CIN3. If left untreated, CIN2 or CIN3 (collectively referred to as CIN2+) can progress to cervical cancer. Instead of screening and diagnosis by the standard sequence of cytology, colposcopy, biopsy, and histological confirmation of CIN, an alternative method is to use a ‘screen-and-treat’

sections.title: Screen-and-treat strategy summary recommendations

summary.text: Summarises the screen-and-treat recommendations, beginning with advice against cold knife conization so that all strategies use cryotherapy, or LEEP when cryotherapy is unsuitable. It sets out the panel's suggested preferences between strategies based on HPV testing, VIA and cytology with colposcopy, including options for resource-limited settings and countries with existing quality cytology programmes. The section also begins the background, describing how CIN is graded by the thickness of abnormal epithelium.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the goal of a screen-and-treat programme: reducing cervical cancer and deaths with few adverse events, linked to treatment and referral for invasive cancer. It explains how single tests and sequences of tests are used and how women with discordant results are managed. It notes that the recommendations rest on evidence about test accuracy and the benefits and harms of treatment.

sections.extract: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a premalignant lesion that may exist at any one of three stages: CIN1, CIN2, or CIN3.2 If left untreated, CIN2 or CIN3 (collectively referred to as CIN2+) can progress to cervical cancer. summary.text: Identifies the guideline's main audience as health policy-makers, managers and programme officers who choose cervical cancer prevention strategies, as well as reproductive health, STI, HIV and family planning staff.

sections.extract: This guideline is intended primarily for policy-makers, managers, programme officers, and other professionals in the health sector who have responsibility for choosing strategies for cervical cancer prevention, at country, regional and district levels. Individuals working in reproductive health care programmes, particularly programmes for the prevention of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including HIV/AIDS

sections.title: Purpose

summary.text: Sets out what the guideline contains: screen-and-treat recommendations, a decision flowchart for choosing a strategy, and flowcharts for each strategy by HIV status. It also describes the methods used and points to online GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-recommendation tables.

sections.extract: This guideline provides recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies to prevent cervical cancer (Chapter 3). sections.title: Formulating questions and determining outcomes

summary.text: Explains how the Guideline Development Group in 2011 narrowed 15 possible questions to eight through an online survey, dropping comparisons not used in practice. It then describes how outcomes such as cancer, mortality and treatment complications were ranked, with those rated important or higher included in the evidence review.

sections.extract: outcomes In February 2011, the GDG met to discuss the questions and outcomes to address in the chapter on screen-and-treat strategies to appear in the updated C4-GEP, in order to incorporate new evidence. The GDG identified 15 potential questions to guide the evidence review for screening options and treatment strategies for cervical pre-cancer. The MG surveyed the GDG anonymously online using Survey Monkey5 to

sections.title: Synthesis of the evidence and preparation of evidence profiles

summary.text: Explains that few randomized trials link screening strategies to treatment and patient outcomes, so the evidence came mostly from separate studies of test accuracy and of outcomes after treatment. It describes the systematic reviews, pooling of data and use of GRADE to rate evidence quality. It adds that evidence-to-recommendation tables were prepared summarising benefits, harms, values, resource use and feasibility.

sections.extract: preparation of evidence profiles A screen-and-treat strategy is made up of two linked parts: the screening test(s) followed by treatment of CIN. sections.title: Modelling of health outcomes

summary.text: Explains that the most accurate test is not necessarily the best choice, so a decision-analysis model was built to estimate downstream health outcomes of true and false screening results. The model calculated these for VIA, HPV testing and cytology, with assumptions set in advance and sensitivity analyses by HIV status and age.

sections.extract: A screening test with the highest diagnostic accuracy is not necessarily the test of choice in clinical practice. The decision to recommend a screening test needs to be justified by its impact on downstream patient-important health outcomes. sections.title: Development of the recommendations

summary.text: Describes the April 2012 meeting at which the guideline groups reviewed evidence on benefits, harms, values, resources and feasibility to agree the recommendations. It notes qualitative evidence that women may fear screening and find a second visit burdensome. It explains how strong and conditional recommendations were distinguished, noting that many in this guideline are conditional.

sections.extract: In early 2012 (26–28 April), the GDG, the ERG and the MG met to discuss the recommendations. sections.title: Important considerations that apply to all screen-and-treat recommendations

summary.text: Sets out considerations that apply to all the recommendations, which target women aged 30 and over with priority for those aged 30–49, noting that even one screening in a lifetime is beneficial. It gives specific guidance for women living with HIV or of unknown status in high-prevalence areas, including screening once sexually active. It also covers screening intervals and follow-up one year after treatment.

sections.extract: all screen-and-treat recommendations Population targeted by the recommendations The recommendations in this guideline apply to women 30 years of age (recommended age to start screening) and older because of their higher risk of cervical cancer. sections.title: Screen-and-treat recommendations

summary.text: Presents the detailed screen-and-treat recommendations, each with remarks, an evidence summary and the panel's reasoning. It begins with a strong recommendation against cold knife conization because its harms, such as major bleeding, outweigh a small reduction in recurrence. Later recommendations compare HPV testing, VIA and cytology followed by colposcopy, favouring HPV testing where resources permit and VIA over cytology-based strategies. The section ends by comparing sequential strategies, such as an HPV test followed by colposcopy or VIA; in the extracted text the evidence-quality ratings appear to be missing from the recommendation statements.

sections.title: Research gaps and further considerations

summary.text: Notes the scarcity of randomized trials comparing screen-and-treat strategies on patient outcomes, especially for test sequences and for women living with HIV. It raises concerns about cytology programmes in weak health systems and discusses other factors such as loss to follow-up. It also mentions possible additional benefits of screening, such as detecting STIs, that studies do not consistently measure.

sections.extract: The best evidence to assess the effects of a screen-and-treat strategy is from randomized controlled trials in which women are randomly allocated to receive one or another screen-and- treat strategy and then all screened women are followed and patient-important health outcomes – such as CIN recurrence, cervical cancer and complications of treatment – are measured. sections.title: Guideline update

summary.text: States that new evidence will be monitored and the recommendations are expected to be updated about five years after publication.

sections.extract: The GDG will continue to work with WHO in an ad hoc manner, so that the research gaps identified during the process can be addressed. In addition, evidence published on new screening and treatment methods will be monitored so that updates to these recommendations can be considered promptly. We anticipate that around five years after the publication of these recommendations sufficient new evidence will be available

narratives.ar: يوضح الجدول ما تعنيه التوصية القوية («نوصي…») والتوصية المشروطة («نقترح…») بالنسبة إلى المرضى والأطباء السريريين وراسمي السياسات.

narratives.es: La tabla explica lo que implican una recomendación fuerte («Recomendamos…») y una recomendación condicional («Sugerimos…») para los pacientes, los profesionales clínicos y los responsables de formular políticas.
narratives.fr: Le tableau explique ce qu'impliquent une recommandation forte (« Nous recommandons… ») et une recommandation conditionnelle (« Nous suggérons… ») pour les patients, les cliniciens et les responsables politiques.
narratives.ru: В таблице разъясняется, что означают сильная («Мы рекомендуем…») и условная («Мы предлагаем…») рекомендации для пациентов, клиницистов и лиц, формирующих политику.
